title: Man with 'ample' record wants to learn Indigenous heritage
article: Eric Nothing's lengthy criminal record is a little longer after pleading guilty to stealing purses from an east-end pharmacy and assaulting a store employee earlier this year.
A judge encouraged the 47-year-old man to get help and make positive changes to his life.

Nothing acknowledged taking four purses, valued at about $200, from Rexall on Trunk Road on March 8 and shoving a worker into the side of a truck when he was asked to show a receipt for the items. A woman who was with Nothing at the store gave him the purses. He left without paying, assistant Crown attorney Karen Pritchard told Ontario Court Justice Romuald Kwolek on Thursday. Nothing was found later in the day. The purses were recovered.
A joint submission from Pritchard and defense counsel Peter Ketcheson, accepted by Kwolek, called on Nothing to serve six months in jail and be on probation for 18 months.
Nothing "does struggle" with alcohol, said Ketcheson.
" Many of his offences take place when he has been drinking and he knows that this is a problem that needs to be addressed."

Nothing is Indigenous. His father attended residential school. He wants to live with his mother in Garden River First Nation and learn about his First Nations ancestry when he is released from custody.
" He has struggled for many years trying to learn more about his Indigenous heritage and, really, where he comes from," said Ketcheson.
Nothing appears in bail court on Friday on other charges. He has been held at Algoma Treatment and Centre for 59 days, or 89 days with one-and-a-half days for each actual day incarcerated.

Pritchard said Nothing has "an ample criminal record" with "offences of violence" predominant recently. Probation orders "have not necessarily been effective in the past." She is hopeful Nothing will follow what's expected of him after he's out of custody based on his wanting to deal with his addiction and reconnect with his Indigenous culture.
Nothing has to avoid three Rexall staff and not go to the business. He must give a DNA sample.
" It's never too late to try and rehabilitate and turn your life around and to become a positive member of your community and connect with your First Nation," said Kwolek.
Nothing declined to address the court.
" I got nothing to add," he said.
